questions.stem: An E. coli culture growing in glucose is shifted to a medium whose only sugar is lactose. Which sequence best describes what happens at the lac operon?
options: Lactose binds CAP, blocking CAP from helping RNA polymerase bind the promoter.
The lac repressor binds the operator more tightly, preventing transcription.
Lactose binds the repressor so it releases the operator, and CAP helps RNA polymerase transcribe.
Glucose binds the operator and directly recruits RNA polymerase to lacZ.
questions.why: Lactose is the inducer: it binds the repressor and frees the operator, while low glucose raises cAMP so CAP activates transcription.

questions.stem: A superintendent opens a bond proposal to a room of parents: "I have three children in this district, and two of them are in classrooms with broken heaters." The primary function of this opening is to
options: establish a statistical basis for the bond's cost.
align the speaker with the audience's stake before making an argument.
concede that the district has mismanaged its facilities budget.
shift the audience's attention from the proposal to the speaker's family.
questions.why: The detail builds shared stake and ethos with parents, positioning the speaker as an insider before the proposal is argued.

questions.stem: A cell is treated with a drug that inhibits DNA ligase. Which best describes the direct consequence during replication?
options: Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand remain unjoined, leaving nicks in the new strand.
The leading strand is synthesized discontinuously instead of continuously.
Helicase can no longer unwind the double helix at the replication fork.
DNA polymerase inserts ribonucleotides where deoxynucleotides belong.
questions.why: Ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments, so without it the lagging strand stays in pieces. Leading-strand synthesis and unwinding are unaffected.

questions.stem: "The budget does increase class size in the short term. But a class of 28 with a teacher who stays is worth more than a class of 22 with one who leaves in June." The second sentence works by
options: conceding the opposing point and dropping the argument.
restating the concession in more extreme terms.
attacking the motives of the people who made the budget.
granting the cost and reframing the comparison that should decide the issue.
questions.why: It concedes the real cost, then replaces the metric of class size alone with teacher retention, shifting the terms of judgment.

questions.stem: A DNA sample is cut with a restriction enzyme and run on a gel. A student's sample shows two bands while the reference shows one band at the same total length. The best explanation is that the student's sample
options: contains longer DNA fragments that migrated further because of their charge.
was loaded at the negative electrode, reversing the direction of migration.
has a higher concentration of DNA, so the single band split in two.
has an extra restriction site, cutting one fragment into two smaller ones.
questions.why: An added cut site produces two fragments that migrate faster than the single full-length band. Concentration changes band intensity, not band count.

questions.stem: "The committee spent nine months studying the potholes and produced a report recommending that we continue to study the potholes." The writer's attitude is best described as
options: dryly contemptuous of the committee's inaction.
genuinely impressed by the report's thoroughness.
neutral, presenting the timeline without judgment.
nostalgic about the committee's early enthusiasm.
questions.why: The flat pairing of study with more study is deadpan mockery; the understatement signals contempt for the delay.

questions.stem: A child is infected with a virus and recovers. Years later the same virus enters the body and is neutralized within hours, before symptoms appear. Which best explains the speed?
options: Innate immunity improved because neutrophil counts rose permanently after the first infection.
Memory B and T cells from the first response expanded rapidly and produced antibody sooner.
The virus was destroyed by the same antibodies still circulating at high levels from year one.
Complement proteins learned to recognize the virus and now act without antibody.
questions.why: Adaptive memory, meaning expanded clones of B and T cells, shortens the lag to antibody production. Antibody titers typically fall, and complement does not learn.

questions.stem: "Screens are not the sole cause of adolescent anxiety, but any account that leaves them out is incomplete." The sentence is most effective because it
options: rejects the opposing view outright before presenting its own.
offers a statistic that settles the causal question.
limits its own claim so the argument survives the obvious counterexample.
shifts blame from screens to parents without support.
questions.why: It concedes screens are not the only cause, which pre-empts the strongest objection while keeping them relevant to the account.

questions.stem: During an action potential, voltage-gated sodium channels open at threshold. Which sequence best describes the immediate result?
options: Na+ rushes in, depolarizing the membrane toward a positive interior potential.
K+ rushes in, hyperpolarizing the membrane below resting potential.
Na+ rushes out, repolarizing the membrane toward rest.
Cl- enters, holding the membrane at threshold without further change.
questions.why: Na+ influx drives depolarization and the rising phase, while K+ efflux later repolarizes. Direction of flow follows the electrochemical gradient.

questions.stem: An op-ed arguing for later school start times is published in a district newsletter rather than a national paper. The most important adjustment the writer should make is to
options: remove all evidence, since local readers already know the issue.
cite local schedules, bus routes, and the specific board vote.
increase the number of national sleep studies cited.
adopt a more formal, academic register throughout.
questions.why: A local audience is moved by specifics it can verify and act on, such as its own buses and its own vote, rather than broader national framing.

questions.stem: Blood glucose rises after a meal. Which best describes the negative feedback loop that restores it?
options: The pancreas releases glucagon, which triggers cells to take up glucose.
The liver releases insulin, which converts glucose to glycogen.
The pancreas releases insulin, and cells take up glucose, lowering the stimulus.
The adrenal glands release cortisol, which raises blood glucose further.
questions.why: Insulin from pancreatic beta cells increases glucose uptake and storage. The fall in glucose then reduces insulin release, which is negative feedback; glucagon raises glucose.

questions.stem: "Critics say the fee will drive away low-income families. In fact the fee is waived for every family below the median income, a fact the critics' op-ed never mentions." The writer strengthens the argument mainly by
options: dismissing the critics as uninformed without evidence.
changing the subject from equity to revenue.
conceding that the fee is unfair to some families.
answering the objection with a specific fact that undercuts its premise.
questions.why: Naming the waiver answers the objection on its own ground rather than merely asserting that the critics are wrong.

questions.stem: A patient's ADH secretion rises sharply. Which best predicts the effect on urine and blood?
options: Urine volume increases and blood osmolarity rises.
Urine becomes more dilute and blood pressure falls.
Aquaporins are removed from collecting duct cells, so less water is reabsorbed.
Aquaporins increase in collecting duct cells, so more water is reabsorbed and urine concentrates.
questions.why: ADH inserts aquaporins in the collecting duct and raises water reabsorption, so urine volume falls and blood osmolarity drops.

questions.stem: "The bill was written in a back room, passed in a voice vote, and signed at midnight." The parallel structure primarily
options: builds momentum toward a cumulative indictment of the process.
softens the criticism by spreading blame across three events.
introduces a counterargument the writer will later refute.
creates a comic contrast between the three settings.
questions.why: Three parallel passive constructions accumulate into a single judgment that the process was uniformly opaque.

questions.stem: Two species share a derived trait that a third, closely related species lacks. On a cladogram, the two that share the trait
options: are more distantly related because the trait is derived.
form a clade that excludes the third species.
must have acquired the trait independently, so no clade is defined.
are placed at the base of the tree as the outgroup.
questions.why: A shared derived trait, a synapomorphy, defines a clade: the species that share it group together to the exclusion of those that lack it.

questions.stem: A student writes: "The author uses the word 'unprecedented' three times." The teacher marks it as insufficient commentary. The student should add
options: a fourth example of the word's use.
a summary of the article's main claim.
an explanation of what the repetition makes the reader believe.
a definition of the word as a dictionary gives it.
questions.why: Naming a device is evidence. Commentary must say what that choice does to the reader or to the argument's credibility.

questions.stem: A population of 200 birds is reduced to 12 by a storm, then recovers to 200. Compared with the original population, the recovered one most likely has
options: the same allele frequencies, because the population size returned to 200.
higher genetic diversity, because the survivors reproduced rapidly.
lower genetic diversity and shifted allele frequencies from the bottleneck.
no change in allele frequency, because mutation rates stay constant.
questions.why: A bottleneck samples a small subset of alleles. Recovery restores numbers, not the lost variation, and drift shifts the frequencies.

questions.stem: "The district cut arts first. ______, it now reports that enrollment in the magnet program has fallen by a third." Which transition best fits the logic of the two sentences?
options: Nevertheless
Predictably
Admittedly
Similarly
questions.why: The second sentence reports an expected consequence of the first. "Predictably" marks that causal expectation, while "Nevertheless" would signal contrast.

questions.stem: An insertion of two nucleotides occurs early in a coding sequence. Which best predicts the effect on the protein?
options: A frameshift changes every downstream codon, usually producing a truncated or nonfunctional protein.
A single amino acid changes and the rest of the sequence is unaffected.
The reading frame is restored because two nucleotides were added.
The mRNA is not translated because insertions block ribosome binding.
questions.why: Two inserted bases shift the reading frame, so every downstream codon is re-read and a premature stop usually appears. Frames reset only in multiples of three.

questions.stem: In a synthesis essay, a student writes: "According to Smith, funding fell 40%. According to Jones, funding fell 40%. According to Lee, funding fell 40%." The weakest feature of this passage is that it
options: uses too few sources for the claim.
misrepresents the sources' data.
relies on a single dated statistic.
stacks agreement without saying what the agreement means for the argument.
questions.why: Three sources saying the same thing is one point repeated. Synthesis requires the writer to interpret why the convergence matters.

questions.stem: A tall tree continues to move water to its canopy on a hot, dry day. Which mechanism best explains the upward movement?
options: Root pressure alone pushes water up the full height of the trunk.
Active transport of water through xylem cells consumes ATP at each meter.
Phloem loading pulls water upward through companion cells.
Transpiration creates tension, and cohesion between water molecules pulls a continuous column up.
questions.why: Evaporation at the leaves lowers pressure in the xylem, and cohesion plus adhesion keep the column intact so tension pulls water up. Root pressure is far too weak for tall trees.

questions.stem: "Every parent in this room has done the math on a babysitter at 7 a.m. Nobody needs a study to tell them what that morning felt like." The dominant appeal is
options: pathos, grounded in a shared experience the audience recognizes.
logos, resting on a cited study of morning schedules.
ethos, established by the speaker's professional credentials.
logos, built from the arithmetic of childcare costs.
questions.why: The appeal works through shared feeling and memory rather than data or the speaker's authority, and it invokes "the math" only to set it aside.

questions.stem: A retrovirus enters a host cell and within hours the cell is producing viral proteins. Which best explains how the viral RNA is expressed?
options: The viral RNA is translated directly by host ribosomes without any preliminary step.
The viral RNA is copied into DNA, which is then transcribed and translated by host machinery.
The host cell's DNA polymerase replicates the viral RNA into new genomes.
The viral proteins were already present in the capsid and are simply released.
questions.why: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the viral RNA, which integrates and is transcribed. Host ribosomes then translate the resulting viral mRNA.

questions.stem: An essay opens with a vivid anecdote, states its thesis in the fourth paragraph, then spends three paragraphs on a counterargument before returning to evidence. The most likely cost of this structure is that
options: the anecdote will be forgotten by the time the thesis arrives.
the counterargument will be mistaken for the writer's position.
the thesis arrives late and the counterargument interrupts the case before it is built.
the evidence will be too close to the conclusion to persuade.
questions.why: Delaying the thesis spends the reader's attention without direction, and placing the counterargument before the supporting case makes the argument feel defensive.

questions.stem: A mutation inactivates a tumor suppressor gene in a lung cell. Which best describes the most likely consequence?
options: The cell immediately divides without any further mutation.
Oncogenes are permanently silenced in that cell.
Cell cycle checkpoints lose a brake, letting damaged DNA be replicated.
The cell's DNA repair enzymes stop recognizing mutations entirely.
questions.why: Tumor suppressors restrain division and checkpoints, so losing one removes a brake and permits replication of damage. Cancer typically requires multiple hits.

questions.stem: "The district calls the program 'optional.' A program that meets during the only free period of the day is optional the way a toll road is optional." The writer mainly
options: provides a neutral definition of the term from the dictionary.
redefines 'optional' through an analogy that exposes the word as misleading.
concedes that the program is genuinely voluntary.
abandons the argument to make a joke about roads.
questions.why: The analogy redefines the term by showing that a constrained choice is not a real choice.

questions.stem: The end product of a metabolic pathway inhibits the enzyme that catalyzes the pathway's first step. This regulation
options: prevents wasteful accumulation of the end product by shutting the pathway off early.
accelerates the pathway by removing a bottleneck.
has no effect unless the end product binds the active site.
acts only after the end product has been degraded.
questions.why: Feedback inhibition at the committed step conserves resources. The end product typically binds an allosteric site, not the active site.

questions.stem: A student writes: "As the report notes, 'the program was discontinued.'" The integration is weak mainly because the student
options: quotes too long a passage from the report.
fails to name the report's author.
misstates the report's finding.
lets the quotation speak without saying what it shows.
questions.why: A dropped quote outsources the analysis. The writer must explain what the discontinued program demonstrates for the argument.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, a muscle cell's oxygen supply cannot keep pace with demand. Which best explains why fermentation occurs?
options: Fermentation produces far more ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.
Fermentation allows the electron transport chain to run without oxygen.
Fermentation removes oxygen from the cell so glycolysis can restart.
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue producing ATP.
questions.why: Without oxygen the electron transport chain backs up. Regenerating NAD+ from pyruvate lets glycolysis keep making ATP, while aerobic respiration yields far more ATP per glucose.

questions.stem: An argument essay spends three paragraphs on cost data. Its final line reads: "The question was never whether we could afford the library. It was whether we could afford to be the kind of town without one." The line works because it
options: elevates the stakes from budget to identity, giving the data a frame.
introduces new cost evidence the essay has not addressed.
concedes that the library is unaffordable.
summarizes the three paragraphs of cost data.
questions.why: It reframes the issue as a question of civic identity, which is what the data were meant to serve. A conclusion should interpret rather than summarize.

questions.stem: Two populations of the same beetle species are separated by a new river. After many generations they can no longer interbreed successfully. Which best describes what occurred?
options: Sympatric speciation driven by a change in chromosome number.
Allopatric speciation: geographic isolation allowed divergence, then reproductive isolation evolved.
Convergent evolution produced two species from separate ancestors.
Speciation could not occur, since a river is not a genetic barrier.
questions.why: Geographic separation, then accumulated divergence, then reproductive isolation is allopatric speciation. Sympatry requires isolation without a physical barrier.

questions.stem: "We did what we were told. We filed the forms, kept the records, and answered every request. And when the review came, we were the ones called to account." The use of 'we' throughout mainly
options: distances the writer from the group being described.
creates an impersonal, procedural tone.
aligns the writer with the accused and builds a sense of shared grievance.
signals that the writer is an outside observer of the process.
questions.why: The first-person plural places the writer inside the group, so the final clause reads as the group's collective injury.

questions.stem: A mutation changes a codon from GAA to GAG. Both code for glutamic acid. Which best describes this change?
options: A frameshift mutation that alters all downstream codons.
A nonsense mutation that truncates the protein.
A silent mutation: the amino acid sequence is unchanged.
A missense mutation that substitutes a different amino acid.
questions.why: Different codons can specify the same amino acid, which is the degeneracy of the code, so the protein is unchanged: a silent substitution.
